subject: PGLS residuals violate Brownian assumption & 3D figures

messages.author: f885e974e72cf61d
messages.subject: PGLS residuals violate Brownian assumption & 3D figures
parts:
Hi geomorph community,

I have 2 inquiries: one regarding 3D figures, and one regarding residuals violating the Brownian motion assumption of a PGLS.

To give a little background, I'm studying brain shape evolution using 3D GM of N=18 mustelid species (relatively small sample size).

First, the easier question. I would love to be able to include a 3D phylomorphospace or 3D plotRefToTarget figure that essentially replicates what I'm able to do in the rgl window -- to rotate, manipulate, zoom, etc. I am aware of options such as taking a screenshot and combining multiple screenshots to create a movie, but frankly, it just does not have the same effect or relay the information in the same way. Do any of you have any experience with saving the rgl output in a way where the 3D capabilities are preserved? I've approached a couple of people with this and had no luck (I'm beginning to sense this type of code doesn't exist yet), but I thought it'd be worth it to ask all of you. 

Second, I'm hoping you might have some further insights on a different issue. I'm using procD.pgls to see what ecological or behavioral variables are predictors of brain shape in this family. I used physignal to check if my PGLS residuals meet the Brownian motion assumption, which they very much do not. Whether it is "regular" residuals or pgls residuals, the K statistic hovers around 0.5 for all variables (ecological, behavioral, body size) with p-values of 0.001 or less. In addition, I ran geiger's dtt function to see if the shape data overall follow BM and MDI = -0.000495, but the plot (attached) seems to tell an odd story (which I understand may be due to small sample size). I'm concerned that I may miss out on important and significant results if the BM model is "overcorrecting" for phylogenetic relationships. 

I have access to code that can help me transform the tree and force the residuals to meet the BM assumption. However, I understand that in other packages (i.e. caper), the pgls function will automatically check whether the residuals meet this assumption and transform the tree as needed. Based on a quick Google Scholar search, I am also under the impression that these sorts of transformations aren't standard practice in GM. Does geomorph have such a function available, and if not, is there a particular reason not to include it? Or is there an option to run a PGLS using a different evolutionary model (e.g. OU)? Are there other ways to analyze my data to still get at the same question? 

I would greatly appreciate your insights.

Thank you,
Ani 

Ani Hristova
Master's candidate
Dept. of Integrative Biology
Michigan State University

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] PGLS residuals violate Brownian assumption & 3D figures
parts:
Hi Ani,

I can't answer your second question, but there are definitely ways to save the meshes you generate in geomorph. I have previously used the Morpho package, command

mesh2obj(x,filename="name")

to save my meshes in .obj format. I believe they have other formats available as well, though it has been a while since I have used the package. From there you can use some sort of animation software (like Maya) to create a 3D pdf, or I have also heard of folks uploading the mesh to 3D model share sites like SketchFab.com and linking to it in the final paper.

Best,
Jasmine

parts:
Ani,

 

Your mesh question was addressed by Jasmine’s response. As for the 3D phylomorphospace, if you first orient it to the position you like, the RGL has a function called ‘rgl.snapshot’ which can be used in conjunction with geomorph for generating an image (e.g., a PNG file).

 

As to the residuals, If they are not iid post PGLS, then one option is to use branch length transformations to attain a better fit. Caper does this using the lambda transformation. However, they are also working on univariate data; this process is less straightforward for multivariate data, and not defined for high-dimensional data (where p>>N).  In short, for high-dimensional multivariate data, these sorts of challenges have not been thoroughly investigated from a theory perspective.

 

However, since lambda ranges from 0 à 1, a simple heuristic approach is for you to try a few values in that range, and then use various post-hoc tests to determine whether any of these improve the issue.

Dean

Dear Jasmine & Dean,

Thank you both so much for your responses! Jasmine, your recommendation addressed exactly what I was hoping for. Dean, I can understand that this type of challenge hasn't been theoretically explored for multivariate data.  I can also imagine a situation where if I hadn't checked the normality of the residuals, I would have just assumed they fit whatever assumptions the test was making. I'm sure as these things are further explored, they'll be incorporated into geomorph. Again, thank you both so much. I really appreciate your time!

All the best,
Ani

Ani,

If you meant a normality assumption check of multivariate residuals, geomorph already has a tool for that.  One of the plotting options for procD.lm objects is type = “diagnostics”, which performs diagnostic plots for residuals.

Cheers!
Mike
